title: Supporting someone who's lost a baby | NHS inform
text:
Supporting someone who’s lost a baby
Losing a baby is a very difficult time for all involved. It can be hard to know what to say, or how to help. But support from family and friends can be extremely important during this time.
The type of support you can offer will depend on your relationship to the person who has lost a baby. If you’re a partner, or a close friend or family member, you may be able to offer more personal support. If you’re a more distant friend or an employer, it may not be appropriate to be as involved.
You should trust your instincts. Your support is important, but you should only offer help that you feel comfortable with.
Practical support
Often, the grief and shock of a loss can make it difficult to undertake daily tasks. Taking on some of these tasks can be a good way to help support someone. Things you could do include:
helping them eat well by providing healthy meals, or going food shopping
encouraging them to maintain healthy
sleep hygiene
taking on some household responsibilities, like cleaning the house or doing the washing
making sure they have enough external menstrual products (like sanitary pads)
making sure they’ve enough over-the-counter painkillers available to manage any ongoing discomfort
helping them keep track of any follow-up appointments and tests they have to attend
looking after their children so that they can rest and process their emotions
Try and avoid general statements like “let me know if there’s anything I can do”. Someone experiencing a loss is unlikely to reach out for help.
Instead, try making specific offers. You could say “I’m in the supermarket, what do you need?” or “I’m taking my kids to soft play, shall I take yours too?”. Specific help is more likely to be of use to someone who is grieving.
Emotional support
Supporting someone emotionally can be daunting. You may feel like you do not know what to say. You do not need to come up with anything complicated or profound. You can even admit that you do not know what to say, but that you want to help where you can.
Someone who has experienced a loss may be reluctant to talk about it. This is likely if they’re not used to sharing their feelings. But, talking does help in the recovery process. You could try:
asking if they want to remember important dates about their baby, like their due date
offering to help them with remembrance activities, like creating a memory box or adding an entry to the
memorial book of pregnancy and baby loss
discussing how they want to tell other people, and offering to be there when they do
acknowledging their loss, and letting them know that you are sorry for it
When offering emotional support, it’s important to listen without judgement. Everyone grieves in different ways, and their feelings may not be the same as your own. Try to understand their feelings.
When talking to someone who has had a loss, it’s important to use the same words they do. Some people like to talk about their loss as a baby, while others prefer to use foetus or embryo. Some people may name their baby and use a gender, while others will not. There’s no right way for someone to handle this. Listen to how they talk and use the same language. This will help them to feel less alone.
They may also question why things have happened. It’s natural to want to provide answers, but it’s very unlikely that you’ll have any. You can remind them that it’s unlikely their loss is because of anything they did or did not do.
It’s also tempting to offer encouragement and solutions. This can be helpful, particularly if you have a similar experience to share. But, looking for a solution can make it seem like you’re dismissing their feelings. It’s important to remember to listen to how they feel and to sit with them in their pain, without trying to fix things.
Negative reactions to your support
When you’re supporting someone who has had a loss, you may face negative reactions to your help. Grief and shock can make people act in unexpected ways. The changing hormone levels caused by pregnancy and baby loss can also cause changes in mood.
If you’re currently pregnant, or have a baby or young child, it’s possible that they’ll not want to be around you. This is normally because it’s too painful to be reminded of what they’ve lost. Try not to take this personally.
You might feel they’re angrier or more distant with you. People often take out difficult emotions on the people they are closest to. It does not mean they don’t care, or that they don’t need you.
Symptoms to look for
Speak to your GP practice if:
You or someone else has symptoms of depression like:
continuous low mood or sadness
lack of motivation
feeling hopeless and helpless
feeling anxious or worried
disturbed sleep
avoiding contact with family and friends
feeling overwhelmed by daily life and the needs of your home, work or family life
If you’re concerned about someone’s mental health, encourage them to speak to their GP practice.
Further advice on getting help for your mental health
Further support
Supporting someone who has experienced a loss can be difficult. It’s important to make sure that you’re also looking after yourself at this time.
There are charities and organisations that provide support for those who have had a loss. You can look at their resources for help. You can also suggest helplines, online forums and support groups to the person you’re supporting.
